sources.text: Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.

Fifth, because the transmitting side of a directly connected link cannot send any faster than the bandwidth of the link allows, and only one host is pumping data into the link, it is not possible to unknowingly congest the link. Said another way, the load on the link is visible in the form of a queue of packets at the sender. In contrast, the sending side of a TCP connection has no idea what links will be traversed to reach the destination. For example, the sending machine might be directly connected to a relatively fast Ethernet—and capable of sending data at a rate of 10 Gbps—but somewhere out in the middle of the network, a 1.5-Mbps link must be traversed. And, to make matters worse, data being generated by many different sources might be trying to traverse this same slow link. This leads to the problem of network congestion. Discussion of this topic is delayed until the next chapter.

It is now possible to understand how a slow receiving process ultimately stops a fast sending process. First, the receive buffer fills up, which means the advertised window shrinks to 0. An advertised window of 0 means that the sending side cannot transmit any data, even though data it has previously sent has been successfully acknowledged. Finally, not being able to transmit any data means that the send buffer fills up, which ultimately causes TCP to block the sending process. As soon as the receiving process starts to read data again, the receive-side TCP is able to open its window back up, which allows the send-side TCP to transmit data out of its buffer. When this data is eventually acknowledged, LastByteAcked is incremented, the buffer space holding this acknowledged data becomes free, and the sending process is unblocked and allowed to proceed.

6.3 TCP Congestion Control

This section describes the predominant example of end-to-end congestion control in use today, which is implemented by TCP. The essential strategy of TCP is to send packets into the network without a reservation and then to react to observable events that occur. TCP assumes only FIFO queuing in the network’s routers, but also works with other queuing strategies.

TCP maintains a new state variable for each connection, called CongestionWindow, which is used by the source to limit how much data it is allowed to have in transit at a given time. The congestion window is congestion control’s counterpart to flow control’s advertised window. TCP is modified such that the maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is now the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. Thus, using the variables defined in the previous chapter, TCP’s effective window is revised as follows:

That is, MaxWindow replaces AdvertisedWindow in the calculation of EffectiveWindow. Thus, a TCP source is allowed to send no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host—can accommodate.

In addition to the above features, TCP also implements a highly tuned congestion-control mechanism. The idea of this mechanism is to throttle how fast TCP sends data, not for the sake of keeping the sender from over-running the receiver, but so as to keep the sender from overloading the network. A description of TCP’s congestion-control mechanism is postponed until the next chapter, where we discuss it in the larger context of how network resources are fairly allocated.

Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.

response.title: TCP Flow Control vs. Congestion Control: Justifying the Effective Window Constraint

questions.stem:
A TCP sender's rate is limited by two distinct mechanisms: the receiver's advertised window (flow control) and the congestion window (congestion control).

The supplied excerpt states: "Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact." It also states that TCP's effective window uses MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow), so that "a TCP source is allowed to send no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host—can accommodate." Consider this scenario:

- The sender is directly connected to a fast Ethernet and can transmit at 10 Gbps.
- The receiver's application is slow to read data, and its advertised window has shrunk to 0.
- Elsewhere in the path, a 1.5-Mbps link is shared by many sources and is congested.
- The sender has previously sent data that was successfully acknowledged.

For the scenario above, decide which mechanism each of the two constraints protects against, then justify why TCP cannot safely ignore either constraint when deciding how much unacknowledged data it may have in transit.

Answer each part:
1. In one sentence, state what the advertised window of 0 tells the sender and which sending process behavior results.
2. In one sentence, state what the congestion window protects against and why the directly connected fast link does not remove the congestion control limit.
3. State the formula TCP uses to compute the maximum allowed unacknowledged data (name the two windows and the operation).
4. Using that formula, justify whether the sender may send: (a) when AdvertisedWindow = 0, and (b) when AdvertisedWindow > 0 but CongestionWindow is small due to the congested 1.5-Mbps link.
questions.answer:
1. AdvertisedWindow = 0 means the sender cannot transmit any data even though prior data was successfully acknowledged; the receive buffer has filled up, so TCP blocks the sending process once the send buffer also fills.
2. The congestion window limits too much data from being injected into the network so switches or links do not become overloaded; a fast local link does not help because the sender does not know what links will be traversed and a slow shared link may be the bottleneck.
3. MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow); the maximum unacknowledged data allowed is the smaller of the two windows (a minimum operation).
4. (a) With AdvertisedWindow = 0, min(CongestionWindow, 0) = 0, so the sender may send no data regardless of CongestionWindow. (b) With AdvertisedWindow > 0 but a small CongestionWindow, min gives the small CongestionWindow, so the sender is limited to that smaller value; the network, not the receiver, is the binding constraint, and the sender may send only up to the congestion window.
questions.explanation: Flow control is an end-to-end issue: the advertised window reflects the receiver's available buffer, and a window of 0 stops transmission even after acknowledgments. Congestion control is about how hosts and networks interact: the congestion window keeps too much data from being injected into the network, and it matters even on a fast local link because the sender cannot see the intermediate links and shared bottlenecks. TCP combines both by using MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow), so the effective sending rate is bounded by the slowest component, whether that is the destination host or the network.
questions.difficulty_reason: Requires distinguishing two mechanisms from supplied excerpts, applying the MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow) rule to two contrasting concrete constraints, and justifying why the fast local link does not exempt the sender from congestion control.

expected_steps: State that AdvertisedWindow = 0 blocks transmission of any data even after prior acknowledgments, and the send buffer eventually blocks the process.
State that CongestionWindow prevents overloading the network, and the fast directly connected link does not reveal intermediate or shared slow links.
Conclude (a) AdvertisedWindow = 0 forces MaxWindow = 0 so no sending; (b) with AdvertisedWindow > 0, a small CongestionWindow binds and limits unacknowledged data.

response.answer:
1. An advertised window of 0 tells the sender that the receiver's buffer is full and the sender must stop transmitting new data, so TCP blocks the sending process from sending further unacknowledged data.

2. The congestion window protects against injecting too much data into the network and overloading intermediate links or switches; the directly connected fast link does not remove this limit because the sender has no knowledge of the path, and a remote bottleneck link such as the shared 1.5-Mbps link can still become congested by many sources.

3. TCP computes the maximum allowed unacknowledged data as MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow).

4. (a) When AdvertisedWindow = 0, MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, 0) = 0, so the sender may not send any new data, even if previous data has been acknowledged. (b) When AdvertisedWindow > 0 but CongestionWindow is small due to the congested 1.5-Mbps link, MaxWindow = min(small CongestionWindow, positive AdvertisedWindow) = small CongestionWindow, so the sender may send only up to that small congestion-window amount; it may not send faster than the congested network can handle.
response.explanation: The scenario asks for a qualitative application of flow control and congestion control to a TCP sender. The advertised window is the receiver-imposed limit; an advertised window of 0 means the sender must stop sending new data and is blocked. The congestion window is the network-imposed limit and is needed even when the sender has a fast local link because the path may contain a remote bottleneck shared by other sources. TCP's effective limit is the minimum of the two windows, so either a zero advertised window or a small congestion window can reduce the allowed unacknowledged data to zero or a small value. No numerical CPU scheduling calculation is requested, so no scheduling tool is used.

A TCP sender's rate is limited by two distinct mechanisms: the receiver's advertised window (flow control) and the congestion window (congestion control).

The supplied excerpt states: "Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact." It also states that TCP's effective window uses MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow), so that "a TCP source is allowed to send no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host—can accommodate." Consider this scenario:

- The sender is directly connected to a fast Ethernet and can transmit at 10 Gbps.
- The receiver's application is slow to read data, and its advertised window has shrunk to 0.
- Elsewhere in the path, a 1.5-Mbps link is shared by many sources and is congested.
- The sender has previously sent data that was successfully acknowledged.

For the scenario above, decide which mechanism each of the two constraints protects against, then justify why TCP cannot safely ignore either constraint when deciding how much unacknowledged data it may have in transit.

Answer each part:
1. In one sentence, state what the advertised window of 0 tells the sender and which sending process behavior results.
2. In one sentence, state what the congestion window protects against and why the directly connected fast link does not remove the congestion control limit.
3. State the formula TCP uses to compute the maximum allowed unacknowledged data (name the two windows and the operation).
4. Using that formula, justify whether the sender may send: (a) when AdvertisedWindow = 0, and (b) when AdvertisedWindow > 0 but CongestionWindow is small due to the congested 1.5-Mbps link.
questions.answer:
1. AdvertisedWindow = 0 means the sender cannot transmit any data even though prior data was successfully acknowledged; the receive buffer has filled up, so TCP blocks the sending process once the send buffer also fills.
2. The congestion window limits too much data from being injected into the network so switches or links do not become overloaded; a fast local link does not help because the sender does not know what links will be traversed and a slow shared link may be the bottleneck.
3. MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow); the maximum unacknowledged data allowed is the smaller of the two windows (a minimum operation).
4. (a) With AdvertisedWindow = 0, min(CongestionWindow, 0) = 0, so the sender may send no data regardless of CongestionWindow. (b) With AdvertisedWindow > 0 but a small CongestionWindow, min gives the small CongestionWindow, so the sender is limited to that smaller value; the network, not the receiver, is the binding constraint, and the sender may send only up to the congestion window.
questions.explanation: Flow control is an end-to-end issue: the advertised window reflects the receiver's available buffer, and a window of 0 stops transmission even after acknowledgments. Congestion control is about how hosts and networks interact: the congestion window keeps too much data from being injected into the network, and it matters even on a fast local link because the sender cannot see the intermediate links and shared bottlenecks. TCP combines both by using MaxWindow = min(CongestionWindow, AdvertisedWindow), so the effective sending rate is bounded by the slowest component, whether that is the destination host or the network.

sources.text: Since many people confuse congestion control and flow control, we restate the difference. Flow control involves preventing senders from over-running the capacity of receivers. Congestion control involves preventing too much data from being injected into the network, thereby causing switches or links to become overloaded. Thus, flow control is an end-to-end issue, while congestion control is concerned with how hosts and networks interact.

Fifth, because the transmitting side of a directly connected link cannot send any faster than the bandwidth of the link allows, and only one host is pumping data into the link, it is not possible to unknowingly congest the link. Said another way, the load on the link is visible in the form of a queue of packets at the sender. In contrast, the sending side of a TCP connection has no idea what links will be traversed to reach the destination. For example, the sending machine might be directly connected to a relatively fast Ethernet—and capable of sending data at a rate of 10 Gbps—but somewhere out in the middle of the network, a 1.5-Mbps link must be traversed. And, to make matters worse, data being generated by many different sources might be trying to traverse this same slow link. This leads to the problem of network congestion. Discussion of this topic is delayed until the next chapter.

It is now possible to understand how a slow receiving process ultimately stops a fast sending process. First, the receive buffer fills up, which means the advertised window shrinks to 0. An advertised window of 0 means that the sending side cannot transmit any data, even though data it has previously sent has been successfully acknowledged. Finally, not being able to transmit any data means that the send buffer fills up, which ultimately causes TCP to block the sending process. As soon as the receiving process starts to read data again, the receive-side TCP is able to open its window back up, which allows the send-side TCP to transmit data out of its buffer. When this data is eventually acknowledged, LastByteAcked is incremented, the buffer space holding this acknowledged data becomes free, and the sending process is unblocked and allowed to proceed.

6.3 TCP Congestion Control

This section describes the predominant example of end-to-end congestion control in use today, which is implemented by TCP. The essential strategy of TCP is to send packets into the network without a reservation and then to react to observable events that occur. TCP assumes only FIFO queuing in the network’s routers, but also works with other queuing strategies.

TCP maintains a new state variable for each connection, called CongestionWindow, which is used by the source to limit how much data it is allowed to have in transit at a given time. The congestion window is congestion control’s counterpart to flow control’s advertised window. TCP is modified such that the maximum number of bytes of unacknowledged data allowed is now the minimum of the congestion window and the advertised window. Thus, using the variables defined in the previous chapter, TCP’s effective window is revised as follows:

That is, MaxWindow replaces AdvertisedWindow in the calculation of EffectiveWindow. Thus, a TCP source is allowed to send no faster than the slowest component—the network or the destination host—can accommodate.

In addition to the above features, TCP also implements a highly tuned congestion-control mechanism. The idea of this mechanism is to throttle how fast TCP sends data, not for the sake of keeping the sender from over-running the receiver, but so as to keep the sender from overloading the network. A description of TCP’s congestion-control mechanism is postponed until the next chapter, where we discuss it in the larger context of how network resources are fairly allocated.
